title: Chayei Sarah: to mourn and to weep (Genesis 23:2)
hookLine: before the cave and the silver, Abraham mourns; what to do when a friend is sitting shiva

lines: DO I GO? WHAT DO I SAY?
cards: A message comes in: my dad passed away. We're sitting shiva at the house this week. And you freeze.
Do I go? Do I bring something? What do I say?
Is it a party or a funeral? On day forty-nine, Abraham bought a cave to bury Sarah. But the verse just before the buying is about something else.
In the old Jewish Publication Society translation: "and Abraham came to mourn for Sarah, and to weep for her." Grief first, then the paperwork. Today: how Jewish tradition shows up for a mourner.

teach.b: Shiva means seven. After a funeral, the closest family stays home for seven days, and the community comes to them. The Torah has an early echo: when Jacob dies, Joseph "made a mourning for his father seven days."
Comforting mourners has its own name, nichum avelim, and the rabbis counted it among the kindest things a person can do. So, the practical part. Yes, go, if the family has shared the times.
Often the door is left unlocked so nobody has to keep getting up; you can walk in quietly. Mourners may sit on low stools, and mirrors may be covered.
Bring food, not flowers: feeding the mourners is the old custom, and in many families flowers aren't. Then the hardest part, what to say. The tradition's answer is surprising: very little at first.

The Talmud teaches that comforters shouldn't speak until the mourner speaks. Job's friends got this right for seven days, sitting with him on the ground in silence, and only went wrong when they started explaining.
So sit down and let them lead.
If they want to talk, ask about the person. A story, a memory, their laugh: that's the gift. Skip everything happens for a reason.
As you leave, many say a traditional line, may God comfort you among the mourners of Zion and Jerusalem. If you don't know it, I'm so sorry and a hug are plenty.
And if the grief you're carrying is your own and it feels like too much, please reach out: in the US you can call or text 988, or call local emergency help.

how: After a funeral, the closest relatives traditionally sit shiva at home for seven days, pausing for Shabbat; friends and neighbors visit, bring meals, often join prayers so mourners can say Kaddish, and let the mourners lead the conversation.

games.q: you walk into a shiva house. the mourner looks up at you and says nothing. what do you do?
o: tell them everything happens for a reason.
sit down near them and wait for them to speak.
start telling them about your own loss.
games.why: the tradition says comforters wait for the mourner to open. sitting quietly is already comfort; Job's friends did it for seven days.

practice: Picture a living room with the chairs pushed together, a table of food, a family sitting low, and yourself coming in quietly and sitting down, without a speech ready. Notice the urge to fill the silence, and let it pass.
If someone you know is grieving now, hold them in mind; if the grief is yours, picture someone sitting with you, saying nothing, just staying.

wordCard.voice: Nichum avelim. Comforting mourners: going to them, feeding them, and letting them speak first.

orig.note: Hebrew: comforting mourners, one of the kindnesses the rabbis praise most.

carryVoice: Your line: show up, say less. Being there is what a shiva visit is for. Day one hundred eighty-two, done.
